🚁 Epic drone flyover of Tesla's Fremont Factory!

Captured some incredible and historic footage today:  Cybercabs actively testing — smoothly handling speed bumps before launching hard down the track. I also spotted Model S and Model X vehicles in the launch area along with what appear to be some of the final S & X rolling off the assembly line as their legendary run at Fremont wraps up.

The Model Y production line was surprisingly quiet during the flight, but I got great aerial views of the busy shipping yard and the factory’s recycling area too.

From next-gen Cybercab action to the end of an era with the S & X — this flyover really shows the transition happening at one of the world’s most important EV factories. Fremont never disappoints!

What do you think about the Cybercab testing and the final S/X coming off the line? Drop your thoughts in the comments 👇

ELON MUSK ON HOW HE HIRES PEOPLE

Elon doesn’t hire based on fancy degrees, years of experience at big companies, or impressive titles.

He looks for something much rarer and more valuable:

“I think it’s a good idea to hire for talent and drive and trustworthiness. I think goodness of heart is important. I’ve underweighted that at one point. So are they a good person, trustworthy, smart and talented, and hardworking? If so, you can add domain knowledge, but those fundamental traits, those fundamental properties, you cannot change.”

That’s the filter.

Talent, drive, trustworthiness, and goodness of heart come first.

Domain knowledge can be learned.
This is why Tesla, SpaceX, The Boring Company, Neuralink, and xAI have been able to move so fast and achieve what others thought was impossible — they hire exceptional people who actually care about the mission.

Why Reusable Rockets Are So Important

Reusable rockets are the single biggest breakthrough in spaceflight since the invention of the rocket itself.

Here’s why they matter so much:
•They slash launch costs dramatically Traditional rockets are thrown away after one use. Reusability turns the most expensive part (the booster) into something that can fly dozens or even hundreds of times. SpaceX has already driven the cost per launch down from hundreds of millions to tens of millions — and the goal with Starship is to get it even lower.
•They enable high launch cadence When you don’t have to build a new rocket every time, you can launch far more often. This is critical for Starlink deployment, satellite constellations, crewed missions, and the massive tonnage needed for Moon bases and Mars cities.
•They make orbital refueling practical Starship’s ability to refuel in orbit (the key to reaching the Moon and Mars) only makes economic sense if the tankers are reusable. Without reusability, the cost would be prohibitive.
•They accelerate progress toward multiplanetary life 
Only reusable rockets can deliver the millions of tons of cargo required to build a self-sustaining city on Mars. Expendable rockets simply can’t scale to that level affordably.

Elon Musk has explained the importance concisely:

“Reusability is the key to making life multiplanetary. Without it, the cost is simply too high.”

Reusable rockets turn space from a rare and expensive endeavor into something closer to air travel — routine, affordable, and scalable.

Every time a Falcon 9 booster lands and flies again, or when Starship achieves rapid reuse, we move one step closer to a future where humanity is no longer confined to one planet.
